inputs.help: Select none if you do not know.

inputs.label: How capable is the importing tool's own solver?

inputs.label: How tightly is it coupled to the rest?
inputs.help: Tight: fast feedback, rigid mechanical or hydraulic connections, algebraic loops across the connection. Loose: signal flow, slow physical coupling.

inputs.help: Stiff: time constants that differ by orders of magnitude, where the fast ones decay quickly.

inputs.label: How long is a communication step compared with the dynamics of the model?
inputs.help: The communication step is the interval at which the importing tool exchanges values with a Co-Simulation FMU. Between two of them the FMU is on its own.

inputs.label: Is this model stiff?
inputs.help: Typical causes: electrical with thermal parts, hydraulics, fast controllers, chemical reactions.

inputs.label: Does the model oscillate with little damping?
inputs.help: Mechanics and electric circuits often do.

settings.label: Interface to use
settings.help: Who integrates: the importing tool (Model Exchange) or the FMU (Co-Simulation).

options.label: Model Exchange and Co-Simulation
options.requiresNote: OpenModelica exports FMI 1.0 as Model Exchange only.

options.label: Co-Simulation
options.requiresNote: OpenModelica exports FMI 1.0 as Model Exchange only.

options.label: Off: explicit ODE
options.help: The FMU solves the algebraic equations each time it calculates the derivatives.

options.label: On: residual form
options.help: The integrator solves the algebraic equations together with the states.
options.requiresNote: Needs Co-Simulation, or Model Exchange with FMI 3.0.

support.note: Model Exchange uses the draft of the FMI-LS-DAE layered standard.
With FMI 2.0 only the Co-Simulation part is exported.

options.label: CVODE
options.help: Implicit, variable step and order (BDF), with root finding for state events.

options.label: IDA
options.help: Implicit, variable step and order (BDF) for the residual form.
options.how: Nothing to set. DAE mode selects it.

options.label: Heun, fixed step
options.help: Explicit, second order.
options.supportNote: Available for simulations (-s=heun), not inside FMUs.

options.label: Explicit Runge-Kutta, fixed step
options.supportNote: Available for simulations (-s=rungekutta), not inside FMUs.

options.label: Implicit Euler, fixed step
options.supportNote: Available for simulations (-s=impeuler), not inside FMUs.

options.label: Linearly implicit (Rosenbrock), fixed step
options.help: One Jacobian factorisation per step and no Newton iteration, so the cost of a step is known in advance.

options.label: ESDIRK, variable step (gbode)
options.help: An implicit one-step method. It keeps its order across restarts.
options.supportNote: Available for simulations (-s=gbode), not inside FMUs.

options.label: One solver step per communication step
Several solver steps per communication step
options.supportNote: WebAssembly FMUs step on the output interval of the model. FMUs built from C code take one Euler step per communication step.

options.label: 1e-6
options.how: The importing tool can override it.

options.label: 1e-4
options.how: Set annotation(experiment(Tolerance = 1e-4)) in the model. The importing tool can override it.

options.label: 1e-8
options.how: Set annotation(experiment(Tolerance = 1e-8)) in the model. The importing tool can override it.

options.label: Handled inside the FMU
options.help: The FMU finds the event, handles it and continues to the end of the step. The rest of the system sees the result at the next communication point.

options.label: Event Mode with early return
options.help: The step returns at the event time, so that the importing tool can update every part.
options.how: Nothing to set at export. The importing tool turns it on with eventModeUsed and earlyReturnAllowed.

options.label: At most 20 per event
options.help: The FMU stops with an error when an event needs more.

options.label: A lower limit, set at export
options.supportNote: The simulation flag -mei sets the limit. An FMU does not read it.

options.label: Smoothed inside the FMU
options.help: The FMU spreads a change of an input over the step, so that its solver sees no jump.

options.label: Input derivatives
options.requiresNote: FMI 2.0 only. FMI 3.0 uses Intermediate Update for this.
options.how: Nothing to set at export. The importing tool must call fmi2SetRealInputDerivatives.

options.label: Intermediate Update
options.help: The importing tool reads outputs and sets inputs at the internal steps of the solver.

options.label: Serialize

support.note: OpenModelica serializes the state only for FMI 3.0.

options.how: Always exported for FMI 3.0. Nothing to set.

support.note: The Co-Simulation part of an FMI 2.0 FMU also needs -d=fmuExperimental.

options.label: Cross-compiled with Docker
options.how: Replace the host triple by the one of the target.

options.label: No binaries, source code only
options.how: OpenModelica does not zip the FMU in this case. Pack it with the create_fmu target of the CMake project in sources/.

options.label: WebAssembly
options.supportNote: Needs the omc built from the Rust port.

options.label: The sources it was built from
Parameters with a literal value are tunable
Structural parameters
options.help: The importing tool changes array sizes in Configuration Mode.
options.supportNote: Array sizes are fixed at export.

options.label: Terminals from the connectors of the model
options.how: Nothing to set. Written to terminalsAndIcons.xml when the model has connectors at the top level.

rules.because: The importing tool cannot run Model Exchange.
The importing tool cannot run Co-Simulation.
Few tools run Scheduled Execution. Use it only when the importing tool is known to.
An FMU with its own solver gives the same result in every tool.
The solver of the importing tool controls the error of the whole model and locates the events itself.
A solver inside the FMU is better than a fixed-step or explicit solver in the importing tool.
A stiff model needs an implicit solver, which the importing tool does not have.
Tightly coupled parts need one solver for the whole system. Co-Simulation exchanges values only at communication points, which limits stability and accuracy.
With Model Exchange one implicit solver sees the stiffness of the whole system. Co-Simulation needs very small communication steps instead.
Loosely coupled parts can each run their own solver and step size.
Co-Simulation keeps the fast dynamics inside this FMU, so the rest of the system can take large steps.
With Model Exchange the importing tool locates every event and updates all parts at that time.
Error control over a coupled system needs one solver.
A real-time target calls one function per sample. The FMU must bring a solver with a known cost per step.
A solver inside the FMU gives an even cost per step, which keeps an interactive simulation smooth.
With Scheduled Execution the real-time scheduler runs each clocked part of the model as its own task.
Tools that linearise or optimise work on the state derivatives, which only Model Exchange exposes.
The importing tool does not read FMI 1.0.
The importing tool does not read FMI 2.0.
The importing tool does not read FMI 3.0.
FMI 1.0 export is deprecated in OpenModelica.
FMI 3.0 export is experimental in OpenModelica.
OpenModelica exports FMI 1.0 as Model Exchange only.
Scheduled Execution exists only in FMI 3.0.
Only FMI 3.0 Co-Simulation can stop a step at an event and tell the importing tool.
Adjoint derivatives are defined only in FMI 3.0.
Structural parameters are defined only in FMI 3.0.
With FMI 3.0 Intermediate Update the master exchanges values inside a communication step.
FMI 3.0 clocks let the importing tool keep sampled parts in step.
A WebAssembly FMU cannot be FMI 1.0.
The importing tool uses the Model Exchange part.
The importing tool uses the Co-Simulation part.
The importing tool uses Scheduled Execution.
Scheduled Execution was not selected as the interface.
With both interfaces the FMU works whichever one the importing tool supports.
In DAE mode the integrator solves the algebraic equations together with the states. Otherwise a nonlinear solver runs inside every calculation of the derivatives.
The integrator uses one sparse Jacobian for the whole model, which scales to large models.
DAE mode integrates with IDA, a variable-step method with no upper limit for the time of a step.
Only an importing tool that knows the FMI-LS-DAE draft can integrate the residual form of a Model Exchange FMU.
An explicit method is stable only with steps below the fastest time constant of a stiff model.
A model that is not stiff does not need the cost of an implicit method.
An implicit variable-step method works whether the model is stiff or not.
Without a deadline, a variable-step method chooses the step that the tolerance needs.
A first-order method is enough to see trends.
A method of higher order reaches engineering accuracy with fewer steps.
Only a variable-step method with error control can keep a tight tolerance.
A real-time step must end within a known time. Step-size control and Newton iterations have no upper limit.
A fixed step gives an even cost per step.
A multistep method such as BDF restarts at order one after every event. A one-step method keeps its order.
Explicit Euler adds energy to an oscillation with little damping at every step, and implicit Euler removes it. A method of second or higher order keeps the energy much better.
Between two communication points the FMU is on its own. With long steps it needs a solver that chooses its own step.
With short communication steps a BDF solver starts again at low order at every step. A one-step method does not pay for the restart.
Inputs change at every communication point, which makes a multistep method restart often.
Only IDA integrates the residual form.
A smaller internal step lowers the error without a smaller communication step.
One solver step per long communication step is too coarse.
An explicit method needs steps below the fastest time constant to stay stable.
A coarse tolerance is enough to see trends and takes fewer steps.
Reference results need a tight tolerance.
Event Mode stops the step at the event, so that the other parts react at the event time.
Each event iteration calculates the whole model again. A lower limit shortens the longest step.
Held inputs are up to one communication step old, which makes tight coupling unstable.
A master that holds the inputs gives the FMU a jump at every communication point. Smoothing inside the FMU hides the jump from the solver.
A master can extrapolate inputs or repeat a step only when the FMU offers it.
Held inputs add an error of first order in the communication step.
A stiff coupled system reacts strongly to input values that are out of date.
A master that repeats a step, to iterate or to change the step size, must reset the FMU to the start of the step.
A saved state lets an operator go back, or continue in a later session.
Directional derivatives give the importing tool exact Jacobians.
Adjoint derivatives give the gradient for all parameters in one pass. Directional derivatives need one pass per parameter.
An implicit solver in the importing tool needs the Jacobian. Without directional derivatives it estimates it by finite differences.
Interface Jacobians let the master solve algebraic loops between FMUs.
Finite differences cost one model evaluation per state, which is slow for a large model.
A binary for this computer does not run on the target.
The target platform compiles the FMU from source code with its own toolchain.
A browser or sandbox cannot load native code.
Source code shows the equations of the model.
Without source code, the FMU must carry a binary built for the target.
An FMU without binaries and without sources is empty.
The names and values of internal variables show how the model is built.
System libraries differ between versions of an operating system.
The importing tool can set a tunable parameter between steps. The FMU calculates the dependent parameters again.
Only structural parameters can change array sizes after export.
The receiver of the FMU cannot change a fixed parameter after initialization.
Scheduled Execution is driven by clocks.
With exported clocks the importing tool activates the sampled parts of all FMUs at the same instant.
A real-time scheduler can tick the clocks of the model directly.
Terminals group the signals of a connector, so that FMUs are connected connector by connector and not signal by signal.
XCP lets standard calibration tools measure and tune the model while it runs on the target.

rules.advice: The FMU carries both interfaces. Select Model Exchange in the importing tool if it has it.
Find out how tightly the parts are coupled. It is the main reason to choose Model Exchange over Co-Simulation.
To find out if the model is stiff, simulate it in OpenModelica with -s=euler or -s=rungekutta. If it needs a much smaller step than the accuracy asks for, it is stiff.
OMSimulator connects and simulates several FMUs. Model Exchange FMUs go into a strongly coupled system, Co-Simulation FMUs into a weakly coupled one.
Cut the system where the physics decouples it, and use as few FMUs as the task allows.
A cut through a stiff connection adds or removes energy at every communication step. A transmission line (TLM) connection, or a master that corrects the energy error, keeps it stable.

rules.warn: Explicit Euler makes an oscillation with little damping grow. Use a step much shorter than its period, and check the amplitude over a long run.

rules.advice: Explicit Euler takes one step per communication step. Choose the communication step from the fastest dynamics of the model, not from how often you need output.
FMI 3.0 export is experimental. Test the FMU in the importing tool before you rely on it.

rules.warn: Tight coupling through Co-Simulation: use a communication step well below the fastest coupled time constant, and a master that can repeat steps.
A stiff coupled system in Co-Simulation is stable only with small communication steps, however good the solvers inside the FMUs are.
FMI 2.0 Co-Simulation cannot report an event to the importing tool. The other parts see it at the next communication point. Choose a communication step as small as the event accuracy needs.
Model Exchange with a stiff model needs an implicit solver in the importing tool.
A variable-step solver has no upper limit for the time of a step. Measure the longest step on the target and leave a margin.
A step with an event takes longer: the FMU finds the time of the event and then iterates, up to 20 times. Measure the longest step on the target with all events active.
With Model Exchange the real-time behaviour depends on the fixed-step solver of the importing tool. Check how it handles events.
